values.title: A letter that arrived after the first winter
values.greeting: Dear Imogen, Tobias and everyone at the studio,
values.letter:
We have now spent a full winter in the house. The second boiler we budgeted for was never fitted, the kitchen is warm by eight every morning from the sun alone, and the children have stopped noticing that their bedroom wall is a quarry face.
You told us at the first meeting that the site would do half the work if we let it. It has. Thank you for arguing with us about the size of the windows, and for being right.
values.signoff: With love from all four of us,
values.name: Catherine Aldridge

items.title: Lime Kiln House, Mells
items.text: A three-bedroom house tucked against the face of a quarry that last produced stone in 1961. The quarry wall is the back of every room. The front is oak, glass and a meadow roof.

values.title: Fourteen people who would rather build less, better
values.text: We are architects, interior designers and one very patient studio manager, working from a converted maltings on Walcot Street. These four rules decide what we take on and how we draw it.

principles.title: The site draws the first line
principles.text: We visit in morning and evening light before anyone opens a laptop.

principles.title: Repair before replace
principles.text: The greenest wall is usually the one already standing.

principles.title: Three materials, used honestly
principles.text: Stone, timber and lime, each left to look like itself.

principles.title: We stay until the snagging is done
principles.text: The same architect from first sketch to the one-year visit.

values.title: Why we turned down the biggest job we were ever offered
values.letter:
In 2016 a developer asked us to design 140 houses on a field outside Keynsham. It would have tripled the size of the studio. Tobias and I spent a weekend with the drawings and then said no.

We had worked out that neither of us would ever stand inside more than a handful of those houses. The practice we wanted was one where the person who draws the staircase is the person who checks it on site with a tape measure.

So we stayed small. We take six to eight commissions a year, and each one has a director on it from the first walk around the site to the visit a year after moving in. It is a slower way to run a studio. We think the buildings are better for it.

values.title: Who you will be working with
values.intro: Six of the fourteen. Open a card to read how each of us came to the studio.

people.name: Imogen Hartwell
people.bio: Trained in Bath and London, then spent seven years on conservation projects in Edinburgh before coming home to start the studio. Leads our new houses and still draws every first scheme by hand.
people.askMe: Ask me about quarries, lime mortar and river swimming.

people.name: Tobias Arden
people.bio: Began as a furniture maker in Frome and joined forces with Imogen in 2008. Runs the interiors team and our workshop relationships, and still chooses every door handle himself.
people.askMe: Ask me about English oak and where to eat in Frome.

people.name: Nkechi Balogun
people.bio: An accredited conservation architect who joined in 2014 from a cathedral works department. Leads every listed building job and writes the heritage statements that planners enjoy reading.
people.askMe: Ask me about sash windows and choir practice.

people.name: Rafael Montes
people.bio: A certified Passivhaus designer from Valencia. Joined in 2017 and has since modelled the energy use of every project before it reaches planning.
people.askMe: Ask me about airtightness tests and road cycling.

people.name: Hannah Whitcombe
people.bio: Came to us from a hotel design studio in London in 2019. Designs kitchens, bathrooms and the quiet details: where the light switch sits and how a drawer closes.
people.askMe: Ask me about plaster finishes and second-hand rugs.

people.name: Sadie Ferris
people.bio: The first voice you hear when you call. Sadie has run the studio since 2012, keeps fourteen diaries and every programme honest, and organises the Friday site lunch.
people.askMe: Ask me anything. I will know who to ask.

values.title: From the first walk to the one-year visit
values.intro: A typical house takes about 31 months. These are the five stages, and what you will have in your hands at the end of each.

steps.text: Three options drawn by hand, then one card model at 1:100 that is yours to keep.

steps.label: Months 6 to 11
steps.title: Planning and listed building consent
steps.text: We prepare and submit the application and go to every meeting with the council.

steps.label: Months 12 to 16
steps.title: Technical drawings and tender
steps.text: A full set of construction drawings, priced by three builders we have worked with before.

steps.label: Months 17 to 31
steps.title: On site, then moving in
steps.text: Fortnightly site visits, a snagging list we close out, and a visit one year after you move in.

values.leadTitle: Three weekends, forty volunteers: how a rowing club helped build its own boathouse

values.title: “Stone tells you where it wants to be cut”
values.intro: Imogen Hartwell talks to the mason who has dressed the stone for eleven of our buildings, in his yard at Corsham.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You have been cutting Bath stone for forty-one years. Has the stone changed, or have the architects?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The stone has not changed in a hundred and sixty million years. The drawings have. They used to come with a thickness on them. Now half of them say “stone cladding” and leave me to guess.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What do you wish we asked you earlier?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Which bed the block comes from. Stone tells you where it wants to be cut. Lay it the way it lay in the ground and it will outlast the house. Turn it on edge to save money and it will shed its face in twenty winters.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: At Lime Kiln House we left the quarry wall bare inside. Were you worried?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I was worried you would seal it. You did not, so it breathes, and it will be fine. The best thing an architect can do to old stone is very little.

values.title: Questions people ask first
values.intro: Straight answers on fees, size of project and how far we travel.

items.question: How do you charge?
items.answer: For most projects, a fixed fee for each stage, agreed before the stage begins. As a guide, full services on a new house come to between 10 and 13 percent of the build cost. Listed buildings sit at the higher end.

items.question: Is our project too small?
items.answer: Our smallest recent job was a garden room of 58 m². We take on small projects when the building is interesting or the brief is unusual. We tend to say no to loft conversions and standard rear extensions, and can suggest good local practices who do them well.

items.question: How far from Bath do you work?
items.answer: Mostly within ninety minutes: Somerset, Wiltshire, Gloucestershire, Bristol and Dorset. We have built further away for returning clients, with an agreed travel budget.

items.question: When could you start?
items.answer: There is usually a wait of three to five months before a new project begins. Surveys of listed buildings can often be booked within three weeks.
